display: Chapter 6: Managing Local Users and Groups

runs.t: Red Hat Enterprise Linux System Administration I | Study

This chapter explains who can do what on a Linux system. You learn what users and groups are, how to gain administrator power safely, and how to create, change and delete accounts. You also learn how to set password rules and lock accounts.

Root can override normal permissions, so use it only when you need it.

Root is like holding the master key to every door and the power to knock down walls. It is needed for tasks such as installing software and managing system files. Normal users can control removable devices such as USB drives, but only root manages fixed hard drives by default. The power also brings risk: root can delete files and accounts or add back doors, and a stolen root account gives the thief full control. Root is roughly the Windows local Administrator account. Log in as a normal user, and escalate to root only when needed.
On Windows, logging in directly as Administrator was once common. Linux allows direct root login, but Red Hat advises against it. Log in as a normal user and use
or PolicyKit to gain power for a short time. If you log in as root, the whole desktop runs with administrator power, so any security hole could harm the entire system.
Work as a normal user; borrow root power only for the task.

A new account cannot log in until it has a password. Root can set any password. If it is weak, a warning appears, but root can continue by typing it again. A regular user must pick a password of at least eight characters that is not based on a dictionary word, the user name, or the previous password. Different UID ranges are used for different kinds of accounts.

Think of numbered seats in a hall: some seats are saved for staff, some for services, and the rest for visitors. UID 0 is always root. UIDs 1 to 200 are system users given to system processes by Red Hat. UIDs 201 to 999 are system users for processes that own no files. They are handed out when the software is installed, and they run with only the resources they need. UID 1000 and up is for regular users.

5.2 The format of an encrypted password and how login checks it
A stored password has three parts: the algorithm, the salt, and the hash, separated by
Think of mixing paint: it is easy to mix, but hard to un-mix. The
is a random extra ingredient. In
is the algorithm (SHA-512, the default in RHEL 8;
is SHA-256). Because of the salt, two users with the same password have different lines in

The salt makes each hash unique, and login compares hashes, not passwords.
